extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans and researchers of television/comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive features for creating or evaluating a satirical early-morning/breakfast television series in the style of Get Krack!n. Focuses on premise, character dynamics, production aesthetics, guest use, episode format, and likely reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire of breakfast television
rubrics_metrics.description: The series is a satire of breakfast television and features McCartney and McLennan playing versions of themselves hosting Get Krack!n, a low-budget early-morning television programme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target the conventions and tone of early-morning TV for parody: mimic the format, segment structure and presentational tropes of breakfast shows to expose their absurdities. Use the hosts-as-themselves conceit to blur performer/character and heighten satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrasting host personalities
rubrics_metrics.description: McLennan is upbeat to the point of being irritating and unprofessional while McCartney is more realistic, but frequently tactless and socially awkward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a clear foil between co-hosts (one excessively upbeat/unprofessional, the other more realistic yet tactless) to generate interpersonal tension and comic friction; rely on these contrasts for recurring comedic beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low-budget production and questionable sponsors as comic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The show is run on a shoestring budget, funded by commercial sponsors who manufacture and market questionable products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visibly low production values and ludicrous sponsor tie-ins as recurring sources of humour; have sponsors and products that are ethically or functionally dubious to satirize commercialism in daytime TV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Under-trained crew, technical problems, and unqualified guests
rubrics_metrics.description: The production crew are either under-trained or employed as part of a prison work release programme, the show is constantly beset by technical problems, and the guests are unqualified 'experts'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally incorporate crew incompetence, live-technical failures, and inept or fake 'experts' to escalate absurdity and create opportunities for improvisation and character reveal. These elements should feel organic to the mock-live format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revealing dysfunctional and sociopathic behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: McCartney and McLennan attempt to remain enthusiastic, but inadvertently reveal dysfunctional and sociopathic behaviour as things go wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the hosts' attempts to maintain enthusiasm in the face of disaster expose darker or dysfunctional traits; using escalating breakdowns can underline satirical targets and produce dark-comic moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest casting and cameo variety
rubrics_metrics.description: The show features many guest stars and cameos from comedians, actors and public figures (e.g., Miranda Tapsell, Nakkiah Lui, Sam Neill, John Howard, Hannah Gadsby).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage a diverse roster of guest performers—including well-known figures and comedians—to broaden satirical reach, create surprise, and provide different comedic registers; casting public figures can amplify topicality and controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode and series format (short seasons, episodeised morning-show parody)
rubrics_metrics.description: Get Krack!n ran for 2 series with 16 episodes in total (two seasons of 8 episodes), released between August 2017 and March 2019; episodes mimic segments of an early-morning show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider short season runs and episode structures that emulate morning-show segments (interviews, demonstrations, adverts) to keep pacing tight and concept-focused. Track and present viewership/air dates as part of production context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for critical acclaim and controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: The last episode of the second series trended on Twitter and was widely lauded as hilarious, ground-breaking, hard-hitting satire, but it also drew an angry response from right-wing commentator Andrew Bolt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that hard-hitting satire of topical or political subjects can simultaneously earn praise and provoke backlash; anticipate social media trending and polarized responses when producing provocative material.
